data.title: Trump blames $6T stock market slide on Democrats' midterm wins
data.description:
President Trump blames the stock market’s $6 trillion slide on the Democratic party’s wins nationwide that saw it take control of both the House and Senate. 

“The Market is down more than 6 Trillion Dollars since the Democrats’ rather strange ‘win’ on November 3rd,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “NASDAQ, by itself, is down 20%. This is 100% due to the fact that the Democrats are ‘BAD’ due to their Anti Growth, and Retribution Only, Policies, and worse.”

“If they don’t change, FAST, it will only get worse. But fear not, our Country will soon be STRONG AGAIN — Lots of good things happening,” the president concluded. 

When stock markets closed on Friday, Yahoo Finance reported it experienced the same drops only seen five other times since WWII – particularly in 2008 and another in 2001. 

The Nasdaq composite, which hit an all-time high in early October, is now in the red since the start of the year. The Hill previously reported as of midafternoon Friday, the index had dipped by more than 4,700 points since closing at a record high of 27,599.886 on Oct. 6. 

Though chip stocks experienced its worst week since the week after the attacks on Sept. 1, 2001, according to reporting from Yahoo Finance. The country’s primary chip-producer Nvidia – which has been hit with numerous scandals over allegations it violated U.S. export controls – has lost about $2.7 trillion in market value since its peak on Oct. 6.

When asked about the market drops, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday its cause could be a “combination of things.”

“We could see that the market sell-off actually began as the Democrats moved ahead in the polls and then accelerated after Election Day,” he told CBS News’s Margaret Brennan on “Face the Nation.”

“The Democratic position on the SI [(Super Intelligence)] buildout has spooked a lot of investors in terms of slowing it down,” Bessent continued. “We’ve also seen some very hawkish remarks from the Federal Reserve. Many people believe that they may be making a policy mistake if they over tighten.”

Tech analyst Dan Ives said the rough week for the markets could be attributed to a “perfect storm” heading for tech stocks. That storm focused on fears that Democrats’s sweeping midterm victories would lead to heightened oversight into AI and data centers.

It also included Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia, according to Ives. The company is facing multiple probes investigating whether Nvidia lied to investors or violated U.S. export controls.

data.title: GOP Rep 'optimistic' about passing AI bill before next Congress
data.description:
Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) said Sunday he is “optimistic” that Congress can pass a bipartisan artificial intelligence (AI) bill before the end of the year, despite a narrowing window for Republicans to advance legislation before Democrats take control of the House in January.

Obernolte, who chairs the House Republican Policy Committee, said lawmakers have made significant progress on the Great American AI Act (GAIA), a package of proposals establishing federal safeguards for the rapidly developing technology.

“I’m optimistic about our chances of getting something done in the current Congress,” Obernolte said in an interview with NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday.”

“We have had major pieces of [GAIA] passed through the relevant policy committees, and they’re queued up for action on the House floor,” he told host Chris Stirewalt. “So we actually could get this done this year.”

The California Republican has been among the leading voices in Congress pushing for federal AI legislations as states move ahead with their own regulations, which has caused concerns in the industry over a patchwork of conflicting rules for tech companies operating nationwide.

“All the 50 states are going in 50 different directions on AI regulation,” he said, adding that lawmakers must strike a balance between protecting Americans from the misuse of AI and allowing the technology’s benefits to reach the economy.

The push comes as Democrats prepare to assume control of the House following this month’s midterm elections, potentially complicating efforts to reach an agreement on AI oversight.

Obernolte acknowledged that any legislation would require cooperation across party lines, regardless of which party controls Congress.

“At the end of the day, anything that we pass, regardless of who controls the House and who controls the Senate, whatever gets passed needs 60 votes in the Senate to avoid the filibuster, and it’s going to need the signature of the president of the United States,” he said.

He noted that GAIA has six bipartisan co-sponsors and that portions of the legislation have already attracted support from lawmakers in both parties.

“I’m optimistic that we can get the job done,” he said.

data.title: Foxx concedes to Hubbard in North Carolina House race
data.description:
Outgoing Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-N.C.) reportedly conceded her race against Rep.-elect Chuck Hubbard (D-N.C.) following a high-profile recount process that saw the longtime lawmaker trailing behind her opponent. 

Hubbard led by 330 votes in the race for North Carolina’s 5th Congressional District, according to the latest reported totals in the recount. Decision Desk HQ, The Hill’s nonpartisan election results partner, has not projected a winner in the race.

“I recently called to congratulate Chuck Hubbard on his victory in this election, and I sent him my best wishes as he represents this wonderful district in the 120th Congress,” Foxx wrote in a statement shared with The Hill. “While I am saddened that I did not emerge victorious in this election, I continue to have great faith in our nation, our state and the people of North Carolina.”

“After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I’m humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short,” she continued. 

Hubbard similarly confirmed on social media on Sunday Foxx had conceded the race “following the results of the recount process.”

Initial results showed Foxx trailing Hubbard by a small margin in the race to represent North Carolina’s 5th Congressional District. She previously requested a recount, citing state law allowing that candidates request one when the margin of victory is under 1 percent.

The Democrat ran on lowering the cost of living, supporting public education, expanding access to affordable health care and advocating against Medicare, Medicaid and Social Security cuts, according to his campaign website. 

Hubbard was one of many North Carolina Democrats who ousted long-term incumbent Republican lawmakers. The Democratic wins in the Tar Heel State are consistent with the overall midterm results across the country, where the Democrats have taken control of the Senate and the House in a sweeping victory.

data.title: Live updates: Clayton calls Trump's trilateral talks 'remarkable'; Foxx concedes to Hubbard in North Carolina
data.description:
Lawmakers left Capitol Hill and headed home for the Thanksgiving recess this weekend after a jam-packed week of moving bills and confirming appointments, as the 119th Congress comes to a close and Democrats take control of both chambers in the new year.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton on Sunday said he trusts President Trump “completely” after he called Russian President Vladimir Putin, a perceived U.S. adversary, a friend.

CNN’s Dana Bash pressed Clayton further, asking if he thought Putin was a friend to the U.S.

“Dana, in different contexts, you can use a different word,” he replied. “The president pulling off that summit, getting the three of them together, is just remarkable.”

Meanwhile, Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-N.C.) conceded to Democrat Chuck Hubbard in North Carolina’s 5th Congressional District after weeks of a high-profile race. “While I am saddened that I did not emerge victorious in this election, I continue to have great faith in our nation, our state and the people of North Carolina,” Foxx said in a statement.

“The peaceful transition of elected office from one person to another is one of the true hallmarks of our system of government, and I am proud to be a citizen of a nation that prizes fair and free elections,” she added.

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), whom House Democrats nominated this week for the Speakership, appeared on CBS News’s “Face the Nation” this Sunday to discuss the Democratic agenda in the next Congress.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who is challenging Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) for majority leader, joined NBC News’s “Meet the Press” Sunday. 

Van Hollen said that Democrats won’t gain Americans’ trust by going back to “business as usual.”

Fifteen senators have backed Schumer, five senators have endorsed Van Hollen and 34 have not taken a public position in this contest, according to The Hill’s whip list. A candidate needs 28 votes to win the Dec. 1 election. 

Meanwhile, some House races are still undecided almost three weeks after Election Day, many of which have the potential to bolster the Democratic majority. Insiders can read more from The Hill’s Julia Mueller on the outstanding contests here.

President Trump will remain in Washington, D.C., this weekend following his high-stakes trip to Asia, during which he engaged in a rare trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton joined several network shows on Sunday, including Fox News’s “Fox News Sunday,” NBC News’s “Meet the Press” and ABC News’s “This Week,” following cybersecurity concerns tied to recent widespread tech outages. 

Follow live below.

data.title: Bessent compares tech outages to vaccines
data.description:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday seemed to compare the recent wave of technology outages at major U.S. banks to the temporary side effects of vaccines, arguing that disruptions caused by cybersecurity updates are a small price to pay for stronger protections against cyberattacks.

In an interview with CBS News’s “Face the Nation,” Bessent sought to reassure Americans about the security of their money after technical problems at some of the nation’s largest banks, including JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, last week left thousands of customers struggling to access banking services.

Host Margaret Brennan asked whether Americans should be worried about the safety of their financial institutions following the outages, which led some customers to withdraw cash.

“I think the American people should think of it as a vaccine,” Bessent told Brennan. “Your arm may hurt, you may feel a little bad the next day, but it increases your long-term immunity and resiliency.”

The Treasury secretary said the outages were caused by glitches that occurred as banks updated their security systems, rather than a broader failure of the financial system.

“The banks have been at the forefront of cybersecurity for decades,” Bessent said. “They experience attacks every day, every week, every month, and they are by far the most resilient companies in the U.S. economy,” he said

JPMorgan Chase attributed its outage Monday to a software bug in its hardware systems, telling The Hill there was no evidence of a cyberattack. The bank said customers could still access their accounts and funds, though some services were taking longer than usual.

The banking disruptions followed a series of widespread technology failures across the country, including a nearly 24-hour outage affecting Microsoft Outlook and Teams and a nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop that disrupted thousands of flights.

President Trump downplayed the outages Tuesday while speaking to reporters in Manila, Philippines, ahead of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit.

“It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and have all the money, things like that happen,” Trump said.

“It’s fine,” he added.

data.title: Flanagan says she 'appreciates' Schumer, but Van Hollen leads 'like an organizer'
data.description:
Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) on Sunday said she appreciated Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s (D-N.Y.) leadership and work in the upper chamber, but praised Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s (D-Md.) bid for leadership, saying that he leads “like an organizer.”

CNN’s “State of the Union” host Dana Bash asked Flanagan if voters will “punish” senators who chose Schumer over Van Hollen in the upcoming vote.

“What this is about is incorporating new voices into the party,” she said. “I appreciate Chuck Schumer. I like Chuck Schumer and appreciate his years of leadership. I simply think it is time for change. In the 2026 election, what we heard from voters is that they were pushing back against the status quo.”

Flanagan said this meant Democrats taking on the Trump administration but it also meant passing legislation like single-payer healthcare and raising the minimum wage.

“I’ve watched Chris Van Hollen lead like an organizer,” she continued. “I’ve watched him lead with courage and heart, and I think that that is what this moment really calls for, and so I am proud to support him and I know that we will all be unified after this leadership debate and conversation.”

Flanagan is one of two incoming senators, the other being Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.), who back Van Hollen for senate majority leader. He told NBC News’s Kristen Welker on “Meet the Press” that the focus is not on rejecting Schumer, saying he likes him “personally,” but “about embracing what Sen. Van Hollen has to offer.”

“This is a guy who both understands how the Senate works,” El-Sayed continued. “He’s been in the Senate for a long time. But also he’s demonstrated the ability to take some bold risks … And I think we have a moment right now where we need to take bold steps. The people are suffering.”

Van Hollen told Welker that his support is “north of 15 and momentum is in our direction.” He added that the election results were about “economic populism,” where Americans “are sick and tired of an economic system rigged in favor of the very wealthy against working people and fueled by political corruption.”

President Trump, facing a Democratic-controlled Congress starting in January, said on Sunday that working with Schumer if elected leader will be “very hard,” calling him “one of the worst [Senate majority leaders] in history.”

Schumer, who turns 76 years old on Monday has been leading the Senate Democratic Caucus since 2017. Van Hollen is less than 10 years younger than the minority leader at 67 years old. 

The Democratic caucus will hold its election for majority leader on Dec. 1. Schumer has the support of 15 senators, while five senators have backed Van Hollen, according to The Hill’s whip list. A candidate needs 28 votes to win.

data.title: US ports face onslaught of cyber attacks
data.description:
A number of ports across the U.S. are reporting an onslaught of cyberattacks amid a growing number of AI-enabled attacks targeting notable infrastructure. 

The Port of Corpus Christi, Texas, which functions as the U.S.’s largest passage of oil exports, said it was targeted with “hundreds if not thousands” of attacks per day, according to reporting from The Financial Times. 

The port’s chief executive, Kent Britton, told the outlet that attacks surged from “known bad actor” countries and organizations that are searching for high-profile targets. 

The attacks against Corpus Christi’s port went after its computer systems by attempting to find weaknesses. Attackers also sent phishing messages, posing as senior executives, to trick staff into allowing them access, per The Financial Times. 

“They’re poking at our systems and trying to find vulnerabilities,” Britton said. “With AI, it’ll only get more complicated.”

He stated the port was seeking additional help from Washington but “if you’re playing defence, you have to get it right every time…if you’re planning offence, you only have to get it right once.”

The Port of Los Angeles – the country’s busiest port – similarly stated that in August it had stopped 120 million attempted attacks into its networks through network exploitation, credential harvesting and malware attacks, Bloomberg reported. 

Executive Director Gene Seroka expressed that all potential attackers “have to do is to get it right one time” and that it was “front of mind every day.”

The port’s cybersecurity operations team has scaled up in recent years, now forming a seven-layer digital defense, he added, per Bloomberg.

This comes after the Department of Justice (DOJ) and Department of Homeland Security launched a hub to fight cyber criminals – connecting more than 30 federal agencies with hundreds of state and local partners.

“It gives investigators tools to triage victim complaints and map the networks responsible,” the DOJ said in a statement. “It also provides a direct channel to the private-sector organizations best positioned to facilitate outreach to victims and disrupt criminal operations, as well as dedicated technical support.”

The port of Corpus Christi didn’t respond immediately to The Hill’s request for comment.

data.title: Democrats are laying off many of the people who just made their victory possible
data.description:
After the 2024 election, the Democratic National Committee’s digital operation was, in the words of one of the people who later rebuilt it, “stripped for parts.”

Paulina Mangubat, the committee’s deputy chief mobilization officer, wrote about it last week in the industry newsletter “Link in Bio.” Much of the creator program was lost, the team was dismantled, and the work started over from scratch. So she set out to build something that would outlast a single election cycle and helped Democrats win back the internet. Then, last week, as Mangubat herself voluntarily departed the DNC, several of her colleagues were laid off.

On Nov. 2, DNC Chair Ken Martin was publicly touting the most successful social media cycle in party history: 8.5 billion views on branded content, 6.8 million new followers and nearly 4.3 billion additional views from FactPost, the committee’s unbranded operation. The team built a network of more than 700 independent creators with a combined following exceeding 175 million, supplied with clips they could turn into their own content and distribute to Americans who might never follow an official Democratic Party account. As a member of that creator network, I’ve seen firsthand how effectively the team gets content into the hands of people who can amplify it.

Then Democrats won both chambers of Congress. Now the DNC has laid off many of the people who helped make that victory possible.

Anyone who has worked in Democratic politics knows that staffing up ahead of an election and scaling back immediately afterward is standard practice. Indeed, the DNC filed a layoff notice on Sept. 14, well before Democrats knew the magnitude of their coming midterm victory. Many of these positions were likely designed to be temporary from the outset. My objection is not that the DNC is departing from a standard off-cycle practice, but that it is adhering to a practice that no longer makes real strategic sense. Digital communications is one area of modern politics where the work between elections is every bit as important as the work during them.

Martin faces real financial constraints. The committee carries millions in debt and a significant cash disadvantage relative to the Republican National Committee. But Martin has already demonstrated that he understands the case for permanent infrastructure: His commitment of more than $1 million a month to state parties was premised on exactly that argument. It was a smart investment. But the logic should not stop at the state funding level.

I served on Hillary Clinton’s digital team in 2016 and have spent a decade watching our party treat online communication as a seasonal expense – something to ramp up in an election year, outsource to consultants and scale back before Thanksgiving.

But persuasion is a year-round endeavor. Americans increasingly form impressions of politicians and institutions in digital spaces long before anyone shows them a campaign advertisement. Republicans figured this out years ago. The conservative media ecosystem runs whether or not President Trump is on the ballot. Its personalities build audiences and credibility daily, allowing Republican candidates to enter an election year as beneficiaries of work their campaigns never had to fund.

Democrats spent much of 2025 lamenting our inability to compete in that environment. Having finally shown some aptitude for it, we are watching some of the people responsible update their résumés.

What made the DNC’s operation work was distribution, not just production. And distribution depends on relationships that individual staffers spend months or years cultivating. So does the institutional knowledge that allows a digital team to recognize why one piece of content lands and another dies, or spot an opening in a news cycle before it closes. None of that is easily recovered by reposting the same job listings in 18 months.

There’s a fiscal case here, too. Democrats spend enormous sums on television advertising to reach voters they have often made little effort to engage between elections. Maintaining an audience is considerably more sensible than repeatedly paying to reach one from scratch.

Martin campaigned for the chairmanship on a promise to break up the Democratic consultant-industrial complex. The Bulwark reported earlier this year that his continued spending on consultants had drawn criticism from party officials. If the committee has to make hard financial decisions, keeping in-house digital talent with a demonstrated record of success should rank as a bigger priority.

The DNC is not a campaign that just wrapped. It is the permanent institution charged with advancing the party’s interests between elections. Over the next two years, Democrats will have to communicate the findings of congressional investigations, prosecute legislative fights, and make their case to voters who aren’t paying attention yet to the 2028 race.

The committee should protect year-round funding for its core digital content, rapid response and creator partnership teams, expanding them in election years rather than repeatedly rebuilding them. Mangubat’s team spent the better part of two years restoring what the party had stripped for parts. Now the party risks doing it again.

Between now and 2028, Democrats will spend millions on consultants hired to explain how we might better reach Americans online. We could start by keeping the people who already figured it out.

Kaivan Shroff was a 2024 DNC presidential delegate and worked as a digital organizer on Hillary Clinton’s 2016 campaign. He is an attorney and senior advisor to the Institute for Education, a non-profit in Washington.

data.title: Director of National Intelligence: Putin is 'not America's friend in Ukraine'
data.description:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton defended President Trump’s use of the word “friend” to describe his relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin, but drew a distinction between the two leaders’ personal relationship and that of the country’s.

In an interview with ABC’s “This Week,” Clayton told co-anchor Jonathan Karl that the word “friend” was “entirely appropriate” in the context of last week’s summit in China.

“That conversation, that picture — historic, historic picture — was in the context of the three nuclear powers, the three main nuclear powers, getting together and saying, ‘We cannot have a nuclear incident,” Clayton said Sunday.

At a White House press briefing on Friday, Trump declined to answer whether he considered the Russian president to be a friend to the U.S., saying he “can’t speak to America.”

“Is Vladimir Putin America’s friend? Because Trump said he couldn’t answer that question,” Karl asked Clayton.

“He is not America’s friend in Ukraine,” Clayton said of the Russian president. “Not at all.”

Clayton offered a similar defense of Trump during a separate appearance Sunday on CNN’s “State of the Union,” telling anchor Dana Bash that he trusts the president “completely” when it comes to his approach to foreign policy.

“The president is the greatest conductor of foreign policy, in a very challenging time,” Clayton said, praising Trump for bringing Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping together and securing an agreement to avoid escalating nuclear tensions.

Trump met with Putin and Xi in Shenzhen, where the president greeted the Russian leader by calling him “my friend.”

“And in that context, whatever language the president wants to use, I trust him completely,” he added.

When Bash asked directly whether he considered Putin a friend of the U.S., Clayton declined to give a definitive answer.

“In different contexts, you can use a different word,” he said.

data.title: Governments fail to reach agreement at COP31 over fossil fuel clash
data.description:
The United Nations’s COP31 climate talks failed to reach a consensus between international governments amid a clash over fossil fuel regulation. 

“I am deeply disappointed that COP31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome,” U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres wrote in a Sunday statement. “I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands.”

“The take-home message from COP31 is clear:  the world must do much more to confront the climate crisis – and it must do it now,” he stated. “The countries that did least to cause this crisis cannot be left to face its worst consequences alone.  This is a matter of climate justice.”

This marks the third time in the climate talk’s three-decade history that international negotiators failed to reach an agreement — first at COP6 in 2000 and second at COP15 in 2009. COP31 ran into overtime for two days following its two-week tenure, but a consensus was still not reached. 

The European Union, alongside smaller countries susceptible to climate disasters, reportedly rejected proposals that would have cut certain protections and favored countries that export oil, gas and coal, according to the New York Times. Leading oil-producing countries, such as Saudi Arabia and Russia, also blocked mentions of phasing out fossil fuels at COP31. 

Other key issues that created tension in negotiations was the amount of concerted effort by countries to wean themselves from fossil fuels and whether ramping up electricity should only be done with renewables or involve energy sources like natural gas, according to the Associated Press. 

Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s minister for climate, energy and the environment, said, while speaking on behalf of the EU, that the final proposal “fails to meet the moment.”

“We will not accept negotiating backward in time and we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel,” O’Brien told a room of negotiators. “We will not endorse a covered decision…that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.”

Turkish environment minister Murat Kurum, president of the talks in Antalya, Turkey, stated on social media, “getting hung up on a single word and stalling the process means dashing the hopes of people expecting good news from us.”

“A system that cannot make decisions benefits no one,” he continued. “If we are talking about sincerity, we must all act accordingly and work together toward our shared goals.”
